# Should I Replace My Rotors

Deciding whether to replace rotors or simply turn them during a brake pad swap is one of the most contentious debates in automotive maintenance. While many mechanics advocate for turning (resurfacing) rotors at every service to ensure a flat surface, there is a distinct camp that argues against it. The primary argument against turning is that machining removes material from the rotor face, reducing its overall thickness and potentially compromising its structural integrity over time. Additionally, repeated machining can lead to excessive runout or heat dissipation issues if too much metal is removed in a single session.

However, your specific situation involves more than just routine wear; it involves scoring caused by metal-on-metal contact. When brake pads wear down completely to the backing plate and grind against the rotor, they leave deep gouges and transfer metallic debris onto the friction surface. This is not merely a matter of uneven wear that can be smoothed out; it is physical damage that alters the geometry of the rotor face.

### Assessing the Severity of Scoring

The decision to replace versus keep the rotor hinges entirely on the depth of the scoring. If the grooves caused by the worn pads are shallow and uniform, a professional turn might suffice to restore a smooth braking surface. However, if the scoring is deep enough to be felt with a fingernail or clearly visible as distinct valleys compared to the smooth outer side of the rotor, the decision shifts toward replacement.

Deep scoring creates a "valley" effect where new brake pads will not seat correctly. Instead of making full contact across the entire friction surface, the new pads will sit in the high spots, leading to localized heat generation and uneven wear patterns almost immediately. This defeats the purpose of the repair and can lead to premature failure of the new pads. In your case, with a VX Commodore where the inner side is visibly scored, relying on bedding-in to accommodate such damage is risky. The physics of friction requires consistent contact; if the surface is compromised, the braking performance will be unpredictable until the pads wear down enough to match the rotor's imperfectionsâa process that wastes money and reduces safety margins.

### Rotor Retention and Mounting Integrity

Beyond the surface condition, there is a critical mechanical concern regarding how the rotor is mounted on the axle of your VX Commodore. You noted that the rotor was sitting loose, held in place only by the wheel and caliper, with significant movement possible when the wheel bolts were removed. This is not normal behavior for a properly assembled vehicle.

Rotors are generally secured to the hub via splines or a specific keyway designed to prevent rotation relative to the axle. While some designs rely on the caliper clamping force and the wheel bearing preload to lock the rotor in place, excessive lateral play suggests either worn splines, stripped threads on the mounting bolts, or a failure of the retaining mechanism (such as missing set screws or a loose hub assembly). If the rotor can move significantly before the wheel is applied, it indicates that the component is not rigidly attached to the drive axle. This movement can cause vibration, uneven pad wear, and potentially catastrophic failure if the rotor detaches while driving.

### The Verdict on Replacement

Given the visible scoring deep enough to be felt and the abnormal looseness of the rotor mounting, replacing the rotor is the prudent engineering decision. Turning a scored rotor will not eliminate the valleys created by metal-on-metal contact, and attempting to use a loose rotor introduces unacceptable safety risks. The combination of surface damage and mechanical instability warrants a full replacement rather than an attempt to salvage the existing hardware.

If you choose to proceed with a repair shop, ensure they inspect the hub splines and mounting points before installing new rotors. If the hub itself is damaged, replacing only the rotor will not solve the underlying retention issue.
